artifactEvidence.excerpt: NVIDIA builds chips, computer systems and AI software. Hugging Face gives people a place to find and share trained AI models—the parts of AI tools that process input to produce a result. Builders can download models from its Hub or connect to services that run them. The catalogue and the computing are different parts of getting AI into a tool someone can use.

Back to AI: Hugging Face’s current documentation describes both a place to share models and a way to choose among services that run them. Suppose a team finds a model suited to turning recorded speech into text. The model still needs a computer to do the work. The team might arrange that computing itself or use a service that runs the model for it. Finding the model and choosing who runs it are separate decisions.

And owning the platform would not, by itself, give NVIDIA ownership of everything people share there. Hugging Face tells users to check each project’s licence—the terms setting out permission to use it. A model being available to download is not a promise that you can use it for any purpose. The video shop never owned every film either. Even if it was very firm about the late fees.

If your workplace is choosing an AI tool, ask the supplier: “Which model does this use, who runs it, and what would changing either one involve?” A long list of models does not tell you whether you can switch the service running them. Ask which terms apply to your intended use, too.

This announcement gives us no verified change to an ordinary reader’s account, price or access. There is no basis here to tell you to move tools today. When a company promises a benefit, separate its statement from evidence that the benefit happened. Practise that distinction in Working with AI 101: Trusting the Output (And Checking It), which explains why a few correct checks cannot establish that every claim is right.

explainBack.question: Why doesn't a supplier showing you a long list of available models prove your workplace could switch away from NVIDIA's computing if the deal closes?
explainBack.answer: Because finding a model and choosing who runs it are separate decisions. The list only shows the catalogue layer. The model still needs a computer to do the work, and whoever owns the platform controls how easy each running option is—defaults, prices, setup effort—without touching the list at all. So the alternatives could stay visible while becoming impractical, which is why the article says to watch choices, prices and effort, not the list.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The answer should use the catalogue/computing separation (P006), the influence-without-ownership mechanism (P005, P007) and the practical-versus-listed distinction (P004, P012).
explainBack.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language; nothing had to be imported from outside the text.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A hospital's transcription vendor emails that its 'open, flexible' dictation tool now runs 'in partnership with' a single cloud company, while its brochure still lists dozens of supported medical-speech models.
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's framework, what should the hospital's operations manager check before renewing the contract?
unseenTransfer.answer: Separate the three layers. Catalogue: the dozens of listed models are only the shelf. Computing: ask who actually runs the transcription now, whether any provider other than the new partner is still selectable, and what switching would cost in money and effort—the partnership may have made alternatives listed but impractical. Permission: check whether the models' licences and the vendor's terms cover clinical use of patient audio. A promise of openness is tested against these practical choices, not the brochure.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Correct application maps P006's model/computing separation, P007's watch-the-practical-choices test, P008/P009's licence-and-terms check to a situation not in the article.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The framework transfers cleanly with no strain; each layer produces a distinct, actionable check in the new scenario, confirming the mechanism generalises.
